title: Git Internals: Objects, Refs & the DAG

questions.prompt: What are Git's four object types?
questions.explanation: Git's object store holds blobs (file contents), trees (directory listings), commits (snapshots + metadata), and tags.

questions.prompt: What does a blob object store?

options.text: The raw contents of a file (just the bytes, no filename)
A pointer to the current branch

questions.explanation: A blob holds only a file's content. Filenames and structure are recorded in tree objects, not blobs.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Git internals are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A tree records filenames and points to blobs and other trees
A commit points to a tree and to its parent commit(s)
Objects are addressed by a hash of their content
A branch is a heavyweight copy of all its commits

questions.explanation: Trees hold structure, commits point to a tree and parents, and objects are content-addressed. A branch is just a pointer (ref) to one commit.

questions.prompt: Git's default object hash function is SHA-__.
questions.explanation: SHA-1 is the default (a 40-character hex hash). Git also supports SHA-256 as an opt-in format, but SHA-1 remains the default.

questions.prompt: At the file level, what is HEAD?

options.text: The first commit in the repository
A symbolic ref pointing to the current branch (e.g. ref: refs/heads/main)
A copy of the staging area

questions.explanation: HEAD is normally a symbolic ref that points to your current branch, which is how Git knows where new commits should go.

questions.prompt: Match each object/ref to what it represents.

pairs.right: A tree plus parent(s) and metadata
A name pointing to a commit

questions.explanation: Blobs hold content, trees hold structure, commits snapshot a tree with ancestry, and a branch is a ref pointing at a commit.
